module_title: Banking and Financial Awareness: History and Types of Banks in India (Level 2)
introduction: This intermediate level explores the detailed historical evolution (from Presidency Banks to SBI), phases of nationalization, and the specific classification of Scheduled, Commercial, Cooperative, and New Age Banks (RRBs, SFBs, Payment Banks). Ideal for IBPS PO, SBI PO, and RBI Assistant exams.

core_concepts.title: Historical Evolution: The Presidency Banks
core_concepts.description: Modern banking in India started with the 'Bank of Hindustan' in 1770. Later, the British established three Presidency Banks: Bank of Bengal (1806), Bank of Bombay (1840), and Bank of Madras (1843). In 1921, these three were merged to form the 'Imperial Bank of India', which was later nationalized in 1955 to become the State Bank of India (SBI).

core_concepts.title: Two Phases of Nationalization
core_concepts.description:
To promote economic equality and rural development, the government nationalized banks in two major phases:
1. Phase I (July 19, 1969): 14 major commercial banks with a minimum deposit of ₹50 crores were nationalized.
2. Phase II (April 15, 1980): 6 more banks with a minimum deposit of ₹200 crores were nationalized.

core_concepts.title: Commercial vs. Cooperative Banks
core_concepts.description: Commercial Banks operate strictly for profit. Cooperative Banks operate on a 'no profit, no loss' (cooperative) principle to serve rural and agricultural sectors. Cooperative banks operate in a three-tier structure: State Cooperative Banks (State level), District Central Cooperative Banks (District level), and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies - PACS (Village level).

core_concepts.title: Specialized and New Age Banks
core_concepts.description: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were established on Oct 2, 1975 (Narasimham Committee) to provide rural credit. Recently, to drive 'Financial Inclusion', the RBI introduced Payment Banks (Nachiket Mor Committee) and Small Finance Banks (Usha Thorat Committee).

important_entities.name: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
important_entities.key_fact: India's central bank, currency issuer, and supreme banking regulator.
important_entities.significance: Established on April 1, 1935, under the RBI Act 1934 (Hilton Young Commission). It was nationalized on Jan 1, 1949. It formulates monetary policy and acts as the 'Lender of Last Resort'.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A massive exam trap: 'Can Payment Banks issue credit cards or give loans?' The answer is NO. Payment Banks can only accept demand deposits up to ₹2,00,000 per customer, but cannot lend money or issue credit cards. Small Finance Banks, however, can lend.

Not all banks are scheduled. A bank is a 'Scheduled Bank' ONLY if it is listed in the 'Second Schedule' of the RBI Act, 1934. It must have a paid-up capital and reserves of at least ₹5 lakhs. Scheduled banks enjoy the privilege of borrowing from the RBI at the bank rate.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: B for Bengal, B for Bombay, M for Madras. These three merged in 1921 to form the Imperial Bank of India.
The capital of an RRB is strictly shared in this ratio: Central Government (50%), State Government (15%), and Sponsor Bank (35%). Examiners frequently shuffle these percentages to confuse candidates.

exam_strategy_tips: Always link Committees to the respective bank types: Sivaraman Committee = NABARD, Narasimham = RRB, Nachiket Mor = Payment Banks, Usha Thorat = Small Finance Banks.
For statement-based questions on nationalization, double-check the deposit limits: ₹50 crores for 1969 and ₹200 crores for 1980.
